clue.text: Trite adage, but has a cutting edge

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for a thing that has a cutting edge

blocks.note: hack as an adjective means banal or trite
a saw is an old saying

explanation.surface: A tired old proverb that nonetheless proves sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is descriptive: the answer is a tool that 'has a cutting edge', so the wordplay builds a noun that fits that description.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacksaw is a fine-toothed metal-cutting tool whose blade gives it a sharp working edge.

clue.text: Husband has trouble, which may be settled

definitions.note: describes a thing that may be settled

indicators.note: to trouble is to disturb, so the preceding word's letters are thrown out of order

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for husband
taken as written

explanation.surface: A husband is having marital difficulties that may yet be resolved.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the idiom 'settle someone's hash', meaning deal with them decisively.
explanation.definitionFit: In the idiom 'to settle someone's hash', a hash is the thing that gets settled when you put someone in their place.

clue.text: Key almost split

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: cleft means split, as in a cleft chin

explanation.surface: A key that has nearly broken in two.
explanation.definitionFit: A clef is the musical symbol fixing the pitch of the stave, such as the treble or bass key sign.

clue.text: Attacks and captures

blocks.note: first meaning: sudden fits, as of epilepsy
second meaning: acts of taking hold, as of goods or territory

explanation.walkthrough: 'Attacks' suggests military assaults, which suits 'captures'; it is meant medically.
explanation.definitionFit: Seizures are sudden medical fits, and also confiscations of property or the taking of places by force.

clue.text: Is no longer providing admission for homeless children

indicators.note: admission means letting something in, so one word is let inside another

blocks.note: the past tense of is describes what is no longer so
providing means on condition that, as if does

explanation.surface: An institution no longer takes in children who have no home.
explanation.definitionFit: Waifs are neglected or abandoned young people with nowhere to live, often street children.

clue.text: RAF cook needs help with chicken

indicators.note: to cook books is to falsify them, so the preceding letters are doctored into another order

blocks.note: taken as written
aid is help

explanation.surface: An air force cook needs assistance preparing poultry.
explanation.walkthrough: Chicken looks like the dish being cooked, but it is the adjective meaning cowardly. RAF is the Royal Air Force.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone chicken is slang for saying they are scared or cowardly.

clue.text: Society member and well-wisher

blocks.note: first meaning: a member of the Religious Society of ..., a Quaker
second meaning: a supporter who wants good things for you

explanation.walkthrough: Quakers belong to the Religious Society of Friends, so each member is one of the Friends.
explanation.definitionFit: A Quaker is formally a Friend, and a friend is also any ally or supporter who wishes you well.

clue.text: Boy goes over an unusually arid place in Egypt

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal order, so the following word's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: a boy's name
taken as written
used as letters

explanation.surface: A boy travels across an exceptionally dry part of Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandria is a major Mediterranean port city in Egypt, founded by Alexander the Great.

clue.text: Porter found gold ring after party

indicators.note: after places the words before it later in the answer, so the piece named last in the clue comes first

blocks.note: a do is a party
or is gold in heraldry
a keeper ring is worn to hold a wedding ring in place

explanation.surface: A hotel porter discovered a golden ring after a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the gold ring after the party. Porter is not the beer here but someone guarding a door.
explanation.definitionFit: A porter in the old sense is a gatekeeper who stands at an entrance and controls who goes in.

clue.text: Limited cure

blocks.note: first meaning: restricted to a particular case, precise
second meaning: an old medical term for a remedy aimed at one particular disease

explanation.walkthrough: The noun sense is old-fashioned: doctors once called a drug for one particular disease by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means confined to one particular thing, and as a noun it names a remedy for a particular ailment.

clue.text: He wrote a letter in Greek to a Roman

blocks.note: pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
Nero was a Roman emperor

explanation.surface: Someone composed a letter in Greek addressed to a Roman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He wrote' defines a writer: Sir Arthur Wing Pinero was an English playwright of the late Victorian stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinero was a British dramatist, author of farces such as The Magistrate, so he is a man who wrote.

clue.text: He's bound to go the match

definitions.text: He's bound to go the match

blocks.clueFragment: He's bound to go the match
blocks.note: surface reading: a sports fan certain to attend a game

blocks.clueFragment: He's bound to go the match
blocks.note: setter's reading: a man engaged and committed to a forthcoming marriage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' means pledged and 'match' means a marriage; 'go the match' is cast like going to a football match.
explanation.definitionFit: The man engaged to be married is pledged, or bound, to the union he will soon enter.

clue.text: It is there for the asking

definitions.text: It is there for the asking

blocks.clueFragment: It is there for the asking
blocks.note: surface reading: something freely available, yours if you simply request it

blocks.clueFragment: It is there for the asking
blocks.note: setter's reading: a punctuation mark placed at the end of every sentence that asks something

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'there for the asking' means free to take; read literally, it describes the symbol that ends a query.
explanation.definitionFit: This punctuation symbol is written at the end of a direct query, so it appears whenever someone is asking.

clue.text: The No. 1 iron in one's hand?

definitions.text: The No. 1 iron in one's hand?

blocks.clueFragment: The No. 1 iron in one's hand?
blocks.note: surface reading: a golfer gripping the longest iron in the bag

blocks.clueFragment: The No. 1 iron in one's hand?
blocks.note: setter's reading: the top card of the suit drawn as golf irons, held in a card player's hand

explanation.walkthrough: Golf irons are clubs; the top card of that playing-card suit sits in a hand of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games the highest card of the clubs suit is often the most valuable, the number one of that suit.

clue.text: Union negotiator

blocks.note: surface reading: a trade union official bargaining with employers
setter's reading: someone who arranges marriages, unions of couples

explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' looks industrial but means a marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a person brings couples together and arranges marriages, negotiating terms between families.

clue.text: Talk with female, the lady of the house

blocks.note: chat is talk
a female name, joined on by 'with'

explanation.surface: Chatting with a woman who turns out to be the mistress of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: A woman's name stands for 'female'; Elaine is a familiar one from Arthurian legend.
explanation.definitionFit: A chatelaine is the mistress of a large household or castle, the woman in charge of its running.

clue.text: Opposed states open engagement

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its beginning, so only its first letter is kept

blocks.note: avers means asserts or states
its first letter

explanation.surface: Hostile nations enter into armed conflict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'States' looks like nations and 'engagement' like battle, but states is the verb and only the opening letter is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Being averse to something means being strongly against it or disinclined toward it.

clue.text: Appropriate fee to be paid

blocks.note: first meaning: fitting or proper
second meaning: a charge owed, such as a membership subscription

explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' could be the verb meaning take, but here it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means proper or fitting as an adjective, and as a noun a subscription or charge one owes.

clue.text: Flattery left him with a nasty hangover

definitions.text: Flattery left him with a nasty hangover

blocks.clueFragment: Flattery left him with a nasty hangover
blocks.note: surface reading: a man who drank too much at a party where he was flattered

blocks.clueFragment: Flattery left him with a nasty hangover
blocks.note: setter's reading: a courtier who flattered a tyrant and was made to feast under a sword hung by a single hair

explanation.walkthrough: In the Greek legend a courtier praised the tyrant Dionysius, who let him sit on the throne beneath a suspended sword, so the hangover is a literal overhanging blade.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary courtier of Syracuse is famous for dining under a sword dangling from one horsehair.

clue.text: Whale comes in for criticism

indicators.note: something that comes in is inside, so the answer is tucked within the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the junction of the two words

explanation.walkthrough: An orc is the killer whale or grampus, a sense crosswords use more than Tolkien's monster.
explanation.definitionFit: Orc is an old name for the orca or killer whale, a large toothed cetacean.

clue.text: Davies seen playing a form of rugby

indicators.note: players move about the field, so these letters are moved into a new formation

blocks.note: a Welsh surname plus a verb, used as letters

explanation.surface: A rugby player named Davies, a common Welsh name, has been spotted in action.
explanation.definitionFit: Sevens is a fast variant of rugby union played with seven players per team instead of fifteen.

clue.text: Use threats and to obtain support

blocks.note: first meaning: to put pressure on someone by intimidation
second meaning: to rest one's weight on something or rely on someone

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests extortion to win backing; the two halves are separate senses of one phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to pressure or intimidate someone, and also to rest against or depend on a prop.

clue.text: Adjustment in damages

blocks.note: first meaning: a counterbalancing correction, as for error in an instrument
second meaning: money awarded to make up for a loss or injury

explanation.walkthrough: 'Damages' looks like a verb, but here it is the legal noun for money awarded.
explanation.definitionFit: Courts award money to offset loss, and engineers correct for errors by offsetting them; both are making up for something.

clue.text: Put one's foot down, when it's time to study

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to read a subject is to study it at university

explanation.surface: A parent insists firmly that it is now time for homework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put one's foot down' suggests being firm, but it is meant literally: taking a step.
explanation.definitionFit: To tread is literally to step, placing a foot down on the ground as you walk.

clue.text: We take turn and turn about in the vessel

indicators.note: to take a turn is to face the other way, so the first word is read from right to left
turn here applies to the word after it, which is also faced the other way

blocks.note: taken as written
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: We take it in turns, alternating, on board the ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn and turn about' is an idiom for taking turns; split apart, each 'turn' reverses its own word.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewer is a large jug or pitcher, a vessel for holding and pouring water.

clue.text: Neat house made by a soldier

blocks.note: taken as written
RE is the Royal Engineers, so a soldier of that corps

explanation.surface: A tidy house built by a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' is an old word for cattle, not tidy. The Royal Engineers are a British Army corps.
explanation.definitionFit: A byre is a cowshed, the building where cattle, archaically called neat, are housed.

clue.text: A French and German issue that's insensitive

blocks.note: un is French for a
Kind is German for child, and issue means offspring

explanation.surface: A Franco-German dispute that has been handled tactlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' suggests a matter of debate, but it means offspring, here in German.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unkind is lacking in consideration for others' feelings, much like an insensitive person.

clue.text: Far from being off to a good start

definitions.text: being off to a good start

blocks.note: first meaning: at a good distance, a long way off

blocks.clueFragment: being off to a good start
blocks.note: second meaning: having made good progress already

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'far from' as 'not at all', which seems to deny the good start; split it, and each half is a meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a long distance off, and also, informally, making good headway in a task.

clue.text: Procure release of prisoner before summer

blocks.note: first meaning: to free someone from jail, often by escape
second meaning: the season that precedes summer

explanation.surface: Getting a convict released before the summer.
explanation.definitionFit: To spring a prisoner is slang for getting them out of jail, and the season preceding summer shares the name.

clue.text: Justify rate

blocks.note: first meaning: to warrant or merit something
second meaning: to be worthy of, as in it rates a mention

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rate' looks like a noun such as speed or price, but it is the verb meaning merit.
explanation.definitionFit: To deserve something is to merit or warrant it, as in 'it rates a mention' or 'that justifies a reward'.
